results.title: Conformalized Quantile Regression: Smarter Uncertainty Prediction for Data Scientists | by Valeriy Manokhin, PhD, MBA, CQF | Medium
results.content: Traditional approaches like **Quantile Regression (QR)** have long been used to predict such intervals (e.g. the 90th percentile of an outcome) by modeling conditional quantiles instead of means. Enter **Conformalized Quantile Regression (CQR)** — a recent technique that combines quantile regression with **Conformal Prediction** to yield prediction intervals that are both *adaptive* (varying with input features like QR) and *rigorously calibrated* (guaranteed to hit the target coverage probability). In essence, conformal methods take *any* point prediction model (often a regression for the mean) and then use a **held-out calibration set** to adjust the predictions so that the interval achieves the desired coverage *by design*. Introduced by Romano, Patterson, and Candès (2019)​, CQR produces prediction intervals that **adapt to the local uncertainty** like quantile regression *and at the same time*maintain the rigorous **coverage guarantee** of conformal prediction​. In other words, CQR “**merges quantile regression and conformal prediction to produce prediction intervals that adapt to the underlying distribution of the data while maintaining rigorous coverage guarantees**”​. Crucially, this method inherits the strengths of both components: The **interval length can vary with $x$** since prediction from the quantile regression may change with features, capturing heteroscedastic patterns just like QR would​, and yet the interval has a **finite-sample coverage guarantee** of (1-\alpha) by virtue of the conformal calibration step​. By using CQR, practitioners can highlight when a prediction is especially uncertain (the interval will be wide) or give a precise range when the model is confident — with the assurance that these uncertainty estimates are mathematically valid. Another study used deep learning (N-BEATS neural networks) with CQR for load forecasting and achieved **narrow prediction intervals with the expected nominal coverage**​ – essentially showing that even complex AI models can be made trustworthy in their uncertainty estimates by wrapping them with conformal calibration. We can easily imagine using CQR in a climate context too — say, training a quantile regression on historical climate data or high-resolution simulations to predict the distribution of future rainfall, then applying conformal calibration so that the prediction intervals for rainfall in 2050 have guaranteed coverage. **Conformalized Quantile Regression (CQR)** represents a powerful advancement in predictive modeling, marrying the strengths of two worlds: *flexible, data-driven quantile estimation* and *rigorous uncertainty calibration*.

results.title: Isotonic Quantile Regression Averaging for uncertainty quantification of electricity price forecasts - ADS
results.content:
Title: Isotonic Quantile Regression Averaging for uncertainty quantification of electricity price forecasts - ADS
## ADS. ## Isotonic Quantile Regression Averaging for uncertainty quantification of electricity price forecasts. #### Abstract. Quantifying the uncertainty of forecasting models is essential to assess and mitigate the risks associated with data-driven decisions, especially in volatile domains such as electricity markets. Machine learning methods can provide highly accurate electricity price forecasts, critical for informing the decisions of market participants. However, these models often lack uncertainty estimates, which limits the ability of decision makers to avoid unnecessary risks. In this paper, we propose a novel method for generating probabilistic forecasts from ensembles of point forecasts, called Isotonic Quantile Regression Averaging (iQRA). Building on the established framework of Quantile Regression Averaging (QRA), we introduce stochastic order constraints to improve forecast accuracy, reliability, and computational costs. In an extensive forecasting study of the German day-ahead electricity market, we show that iQRA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art postprocessing methods in terms of both reliability and sharpness. It produces well-calibrated prediction intervals across multiple confidence levels, providing superior reliability to all benchmark methods, particularly coverage-based conformal prediction. In addition, isotonic regularization decreases the complexity of the quantile regression problem and offers a hyperparameter-free approach to variable selection. :   10.48550/arXiv.2507.15079.
